finding: The live range of $220-$775 is about right. Built totals for the front axle (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $196-$520 (0.8-1.5 hr); midsize 2016 Camry about $206-$545 (0.8-1.5 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $353-$710 (1.0-1.5 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $275-$468 (0.7-1.5 hr). The live floor of $220 sits just above our lowest totals ($196-$206), and those use an aftermarket kit at an online sale price plus a manufacturer warranty time, both less than a shop normally charges; AAA and KBB start at $250. The live top of $775 covers our highest total (truck with list-price Ford parts, about $710) with a little room. The BMW total is understated at the top: its parts figures are aftermarket and original-supplier kits only ($191-$228); genuine BMW rotors alone are about $230 a pair and no genuine pad price was found, so a dealer job with genuine parts, wear sensors and a higher labor rate can plausibly exceed $775. How solid the labor times are: none is a stated time for the exact example vehicle. The low ends are manufacturer warranty times for other vehicles: 0.8 hr for front pads on a 2003-2008 Corolla (earlier generation, pads only), 0.8 hr for the front pad operation on a 2011-2016 Sienna in a bulletin whose repair also fits new discs, and 0.7 hr (0.4 discs + 0.3 pads) on a 2013-2016 Acura RDX standing in for the BMW, because BMW's bulletins refer dealers to its own labor system instead of printing a time. The truck low end is a parts seller's 1-hour install estimate. Every high end is the same single figure: a technician-run advice site's 1.5 hr (1.0 for pads plus 0.5 for rotors) on a 2019 Honda Odyssey, supported loosely by The Drive's 'an hour per axle'. Seized hardware, rust or caliper work will push real jobs past 1.5 hr. Our mainstream totals sit below RepairPal's $574-$698; the gap is mostly parts (our low ends are online kit prices of $100-$233, RepairPal's parts figure is $406-$452). No change to the live range is supported by this evidence.
extras: Quotes often add: brake hardware/clip kit and pad-wear sensors (European cars), brake fluid flush, caliper service or replacement if seized or leaking, rotor machining instead of replacement, shop supplies and disposal fees, inspection or diagnosis fee, and sales tax. The rear axle is priced separately.
